thread.title: S&P 500 Weekly Update: 2019 Looks To Be A Very Difficult Year To Navigate

author: Fear & Greed Trader
title: S&P 500 Weekly Update: 2019 Looks To Be A Very Difficult Year To Navigate
text:
"Flexibility requires an open mind and a welcoming of new alternatives." - Deborah Day
"You can choose between having an open mind and being a skeptic. There is no in-between." - Brownell Landrum
The 2019 economic outlook is dominated by some of the same key themes of a year ago. The coming year also adds uncertainty with the Federal Reserve and trade policies. In addition, there is plenty of talk about the upcoming recession that many seem a foregone conclusion in 2019. If not a recession, then growth slowing to the 1-2% range for GDP. Not many believe the earnings forecasts are valid, so the overvaluation theme is back on the table.
Global growth is slowing, the Eurozone political situation rivals the issues here in the U.S., and the experts are once again calling for a hard landing for China. Crude oil has dropped rapidly reminding everyone what took place with the stock market in late 2015, early 2016. The consensus is that President Trump won't be able to escape what Special Counsel Mueller has unearthed. And even if he can, there is a group of politicians that intends to make life miserable for the administration.
If you didn't get a pair of earmuffs during the holidays, I suggest you go out and purchase a pair immediately. 2019 will be filled with noise that will make prior years look like a soundproof booth.
On top of all of that sits a poor technical picture. For the first time in years, we enter a year with no discernible long-term trend firmly in place. Given all of that, it seems like there HAS to be a brutal Bear market during the upcoming year. Those calling for that scenario are already beating their chest. After all, the indices already have a head start with the sell-off during the fourth quarter of 2018.
When I sat down to assemble an outlook for the upcoming year, I concluded that it simply couldn't be done. Let me clarify, it couldn't be done with conviction. So as we all read what the many analysts and investment firms are forecasting for the stock market in 2019, I simply sit back and read them like every other investor and form some opinions.
Before anyone concludes that with all of the negatives around I simply wasn't capable of presenting a Bearish scenario, think again. When I have all of the pieces to the puzzle lined up in front of me and they point in that direction, I can be as negative as any perma bear. Despite what may seem so obvious to many, the way I see it we don't have that scenario in place yet to make a flat out call in either direction.
Hence my hesitation to put forth a prognostication for the year just because we have turned the page on the calendar. The market is trying to form some sort of bottom that can be relied on. It is in the very early stages of doing that, and we have seen how any bottoming process is a very difficult situation to predict.
Despite all the negativity that surrounds investors, believe it or not there are some positives. Along with those positives, there is also the notion that every issue does NOT turn out to be the dire situation that everyone is predicting. In fact, most never materialize at all. It's time to add that overall sentiment is at lows last seen during the financial crisis. People simply don't want to own stocks now. Interpret that data point any way you wish, but I would rather not run with a crowd when emotion is clearly in control.
Forget about what many are saying about this system or that system being the next version of the Ten Commandments for investing in equities. Nothing is cast in stone when it comes to investing. The system that is best deployed is one that uses ALL of the data. Then measuring that data with an OPEN mind. No preconceived notions, no guesses, no wild conjecture. When I review my strategy today, there exists a missing piece that needs to fill the void in trying to come up with a plan worthy of conviction.
We may have that answer soon.
Economy Scott Grannis give us his latest view on the economy in four easy-to-read charts.
IHS Markit final U.S. Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index posted 53.8 in December, down from 55.3 in November. That is a 15-month low. Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at IHS Markit:
"Manufacturers reported a weakened pace of expansion at the end of 2018, and grew less upbeat about prospects for 2019. Output and order books grew at the slowest rates for over a year and optimism about the outlook slumped to its gloomiest for over two years. The month rounds of a fourth quarter in which manufacturing production is indicated to have risen at only a modest annualized rate of about 1%."
"Some of the weakness is due to capacity constraints, with producers again reporting widespread difficulties in finding suitable staff and sourcing sufficient quantities of inputs. However, the survey also revealed signs of slower demand growth from customers, as well as rising concerns over the impact of tariffs. Just over two thirds of manufacturers reporting higher costs attributed the rise in prices to tariffs."
ISM plunged to a 2-year low of 54.1 from 59.3 in November and 57.7 in October versus a 14-year high of 61.4 in August. The ISM is now below the prior 9-month low of 57.3 last April, though still well above the 47.8 expansion-low in January of 2016 that reflected the last big downswing for petroleum prices.
December vehicle sales are running at a 17.4 M rate, with Ford (NYSE: F ), Chrysler (NYSE: FCAU ), Toyota (NYSE: TM ), Honda (NYSE: HMC ) and Nissan ( OTCPK:NSANY ) reporting, following the same pace in November and 17.5 M in October. This translates to an average pace of 17.2 M in 2018, slightly above the 17.1 M in 2017 but below the 17.5 M clip in 2016. A flat tend for sure but the "rollover" commentary remains premature as it has been for six months now.
Non-farm payrolls jumped 312k in December after revised gains of 176k in November (was 155k) and 274k in October (was 237k), for a net 58k gain. The unemployment rate rose to 3.9% versus 3.7%. Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% versus 0.2% previously for a 3.2% y/y pace versus 3.1% y/y.
Global Economy J.P. Morgan Global Manufacturing PMI continued to register a subdued performance at the close of 2018. The reading fell to a 27-month low of 51.5 in December, down from 52.0 in November. The average reading over the fourth quarter (51.8) was the lowest since quarter three of 2016.
David Hensley, Director of Global Economic Coordination at J.P. Morgan:
"The December PMI surveys signaled that the global manufacturing sector ended 2018 on a subdued footing. Output growth remained stubbornly low, rates of increase in new orders and employment slowed and international trade flows deteriorated. The outlook also remains relatively lackluster, as business confidence dropped to its lowest level in the series history."
IHS Markit Eurozone Manufacturing PMI rolls in at 51.4 in December, down from the November print of 51.8. Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at IHS Markit:
"A disappointing December rounds off a year in which a manufacturing boom faded away to near stagnation. The weakness of the recent survey data in fact raises the possibility that the goods producing sector could even act as a drag on the overall economy in the fourth quarter, representing a marked contrast to the growth surge seen this time last year. The last three months of 2018 saw manufacturers report the worst quarterly performance in terms of production since the second quarter of 2013."
The headlines read; Chinese Manufacturing PMI Drops to Lowest Level Since 2016 . The 49.4 manufacturing gauge in December was the weakest since February of 2016, and only the 14th month since 2010 where the gauge has registered contraction.
Chinese Services PMI rose to a reading of 53.8 from the prior report of 53.4 and beat expectations (53.2).
Is this all about trade issues or is it also being impacted by China's ongoing transition from a manufacturing economy to one that is more services oriented?
Nikkei India Manufacturing PMI came in subdued at 53.2 in December, from 54.0 in November. Pollyanna De Lima, Principal Economist at IHS Markit:
"The Indian Manufacturing PMI indicated that the sector ended 2018 on a high, with growth stronger than seen at the start of the year. Output continued to rise strongly, in line with a robust upswing in sales. Companies benefited from rising international demand for Indian goods, as export orders expanded for the fourteenth straight month."
"It's particularly encouraging to see the quarterly PMI average climb to its highest mark since Q3 FY 2012, suggesting that the sector made a robust contribution to GDP."
UK Manufacturing PMI comes in at 54.2 in December, a six-month high. That is up from 53.6 in November. Rob Dobson, Director at IHS Markit, which compiles the survey:
"December saw the UK PMI rise to a six-month high, following short-term boosts to inventory holdings and inflows of new business as companies stepped up their preparations for a potentially disruptive Brexit."
"Stocks of purchases and finished goods both rose at near survey-record rates, while stock-piling by customers at home and abroad took new orders growth to a ten-month high. Any positive impact on the PMI is likely to be short-lived, however, as any gains in the near-term are reversed later in 2019 when safety stocks are eroded or become obsolete."
Earnings Observations In early 2018, the S&P 500 was trading at 23 times trailing earnings. Multiples have contracted significantly to the current level of about 17-18x. Forward PE multiples are at 14.5x, which is below the historical average. For Q4 2018 and the first three quarters of 2019, analysts are expecting earnings of $169-170, which works out to a P/E of about 15.5.
It is always questionable to try and place a value on future earnings, as we know all too well that analysts have a tendency to be overly optimistic in their assumptions when things are going well, and too pessimistic when things are bad.
2019 presents more of a challenge than in years past. The threat of a looming trade war and other geopolitical issues as well as a slowing global economy are all huge unknowns. Bears also argue the boost of tax cuts on EPS growth won't repeat.
Then there is the U.S. dollar issue. Companies in the S&P derive about half of their sales from outside of the U.S. When the dollar rises in value, the value of sales earned abroad (in foreign currency) falls. If foreign sales grow 5%, but the dollar gains 5% against other currencies, then sales growth will be zero in dollar terms.
Sounds bleak, but what if the Bear scenario is overstated? What if earnings aren't great, but they aren't terrible either? I'm keeping an open mind.
Hitching your investment wagon to a wildly bearish view or a wildly bullish outlook for corporate earnings could be a huge mistake as we enter 2019.
The Political Scene The state of affairs in Washington has truly become controversial. It's easy to take sides depending on your political views. Mixing that with an investment strategy can backfire. Just as there were members of the GOP who vowed never to go along with anything President Obama proposed, there are also members of the Democratic Party who will do anything in their power to prevent President Trump from moving any legislation. So there is nothing new on that front.
Now that Democrats have control of the House for the next two years, the base case is that hearings and investigations will take the spotlight and little in the way of legislation will be passed. On the bright side, gridlock is supposed to be good.
On the other hand, if any one of these investigations turn up something on the President that is legitimate, it will be a market-moving event. Before anyone decides to sell their stocks because of that concern, please go back and take a look at how the stock market reacted after the initial knee-jerk reaction when president Clinton was impeached. Back then it was about the economy, and IF this economy remains stable, we might expect the same results.
The third year of a President's tenure has historically been a strong one, but it has been far from a straight line higher either. Of the four years, the third year stands out. The S&P 500 has averaged a gain of 12.8% with positive returns over 80% of the time. Then there is the argument that this administration is quite different, and that mixes politics and investment strategy. Best of luck with that.
The Fed For weeks, I have been saying the experts that were telling investors the Fed was hell bent on raising rates and would not stop until the economy was in shambles were terribly wrong.
The stock market is made up of investors that at times act like children. They need to be told over and over again to be patient, "wait and see" before they run across the street and get run over. We saw that play out again as the Fed gave its "patience and flexible" view to the market on Friday.
Sentiment Whenever you talk about investor sentiment, the two most widely quoted measures are the weekly surveys from Investors Intelligence and the American Association of Individual Investors . The former measures sentiment levels of newsletter writers, while the latter is a barometer of sentiment among individual investors.
Combining the current sentiment readings from the Investors Intelligence and AAII surveys and averaging them out, bullish sentiment has dipped down to just less than a third of those polled at 33%. While this is far from the lowest reading of the current cycle dating back to 2009, it is one of the lowest of the last few years. The last time the average bullish reading from the two surveys was lower than it got in the last few weeks of 2018 was coming out of the correction in early 2016.
Crude Oil The EIA weekly inventory report showed inventories were unchanged for the second week in a row. At 441.4 million barrels, U.S. crude oil inventories remain about 8%, above the five-year average for this time of year. Total motor gasoline inventories increased by 6.9 million barrels last week and are about 5% above the five-year average for this time of year.
Crude oil remains below the $50 mark, but is taking a run to get back over that level. That $50 price was once support; it now will act as resistance. WTI closed the week at $48.31, up $3.02.
The Technical Picture The WEEKLY chart of the S&P gives an investor a nice picture of a support area that came into play recently. The 200 WEEK moving average acted as support back in 2016 and so far that has held during this corrective phase.
Chart courtesy of FreeStockCharts.com
Looking at the shorter-term view, the S&P is right at resistance now at S&P 2,530-2,540. There could be more backing and filling before that initial resistance is overcome, or a failure that takes the index down again. An emotional scene now, with violent moves in both direction. For now I will view the low of this past week at S&P 2,443 as the first line of short-term support.
S&P 2,600-2,650 looms as very stubborn resistance. The 20 MONTH moving average is 2658. Therein lies the first true test where investors may get some answers on what develops in the intermediate term.
This past year was interesting and the first few days of trading in 2019 haven't disappointed anyone that believes volatility will remain in place for a while. Two days of news regarding the Chinese economic slowdown, followed by the Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) guidance kept the negative mindset in place. Then positive commentary out of the Fed and stocks ripped higher.
Plenty of investors are getting caught in the whipsaw action of the equity market. As I started to put forth a strategy for the coming year, I concluded that it simply doesn't pay to get too Bearish nor too Bullish especially when we don't have a firmly established trend in place now. In my view, the S&P remains in Limbo as it closed the month of December below what I view as a critical level, the 20-MONTH moving average.
The equity market is in the midst of what could be a transition from Bull to Bear as the long-term trend is in question now. At some point, a retest of the bullish trend will be in the cards, and that may tell us what trend will be in force as the year takes shape. The major LT trend line is in "No Man's land", and could break either way. We can line up the pros and cons as we look ahead into 2019, make assumptions and assign probabilities to formulate a forecast. Rest assured the tiebreaker will be how the technical picture plays out.
There are indications that this could be a replay of what investors saw in 2015/2016. A global growth scare back then that put the long-term trend in jeopardy. The equity market righted itself and new highs were achieved. That does not mean that I see new highs ahead in the intermediate term. It infers that the trend has a decent chance of stabilizing, instead of falling into full fledged Bear mode.
All during 2018 there has been plenty of criticism leveled at those that don't employ hedges as they watch stocks fall. So there is no misunderstanding, that is MY choice as well. That decision is based on participating with a certain level of conviction in a firmly established trend. One might say another reason was highlighted and put on display during this mini rally off the lows. It was also showcased in February 2018 when the market rallied off the floor to once again post new highs. All one needs to do is look at Friday's market action and also remember the quick violent mini rallies that we have seen since early 2018. That should be enough of a clue on why that particular strategy is employed.
Sorry, if I am a skeptic, maybe I have seen too many market cycles. More often than not hedging is simply a waste of time and money. Enormous amounts of money is tossed around as one tries to buy protection . I am hard pressed to believe that the hedgers have the god-like ability to know exactly when to put them on and take them off. It is a mind game that one need not get involved in.
Oh sure, everyone is a perfect market timer. That's an absurd and unbelievable assertion to make when we view the violent market activity lately. All of the talk about hedging is nice in hindsight. It is fantasy to tell anyone they are sitting through market action on Friday with their short positions in place, and not feeling like their insides are being torn out. Not to mention the nightmare of hedging and then watching new market highs achieved.
I cannot say if this rally extends or not, no one can, but I do know it is impossible to outthink the stock market. In my view it is far better to ride out the volatility making the necessary changes that each needs to employ based on their situation while we wait for a firmly established trend to tell us what direction the equity market will take in the intermediate term.
Time will tell. In the meantime, while we have turned the page on the calendar, we shouldn't necessarily change the strategies that have set the Bulls up in a position that not too many others enjoy now.
I would also like to take a moment and remind all of the readers of an important issue. In these types of forums, readers bring a host of situations and variables to the table when visiting these articles. Therefore it is impossible to pinpoint what may be right for each situation. Please keep that in mind when forming your investment strategy.
